artworks.title: The Danaides Killing Their Husbands
artworks.description: BnF Français 874 (fol. 170v) stages the wedding-night massacre of Aegyptus' fifty sons — the bridegrooms cut down in their beds by Danaus' daughters. The miniature is the visual afterlife of Aegyptus' claim: his line dies in Argos so that Danaus' may rule.

artworks.title: Plate with Hypermnestra Watching Lynceus Take Her Father's Crown
artworks.description: Xanto's maiolica plate (Walters Art Museum 48.1324) shows Lynceus — Aegyptus' sole surviving son — seizing Danaus' crown while Hypermnestra looks on. The Urbino workshop turns the myth's aftermath into tableware: the one son who escaped the knives and avenged his brothers.

artworks.title: The Danaides in Hell
artworks.description: Bertin's underworld canvas shows the Danaids at their leaking vessels — eternal labour for murdering Aegyptus' sons on their wedding night. The French baroque scene keeps Aegyptus present as the bereaved twin: his fifty heirs become the crime that fills Tartarus with water that never stays.

music.title: Les Danaïdes
music.description: Salieri's opera needs Aegyptus' fifty sons as the bridegrooms — the twin brother's claim that drives Danaus' flight and the wedding-night massacre.

popCulture.title: The Suppliants
popCulture.creator: Aeschylus
popCulture.description: Aeschylus keeps Aegyptus offstage but present: his sons pursue the Danaids to Argos, and the king's will is the force the suppliants flee.

popCulture.title: Aegyptus
popCulture.description: The eponymous twin of Danaus — king of Egypt whose fifty sons chase the fifty Danaids — remains the other half of the Argive foundation myth.

popCulture.title: Danaïdes
popCulture.description: The murdered sons of Aegyptus haunt the Danaid story: their wedding night becomes the underworld's leaking jars, and his name survives in their crime.
